content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
The paper theoretically investigates whether  generative models can universally approximate any compact smooth manifold.

Although I think this paper has some interesting observations, I think it has very little significance for generative models as it ignores the distribution over the image completely.  

I must note that I am not familiar enough with the related work to judge the novelty of this work.

Detailed remarks:
- The paper claims to talk about generative models, but it actually only talks about GANs. The paper needs to make this clear as this is misleading.
- One severe limitation of this work is that it only looks at the output set and says nothing about the distribution induced on it by the mapping (or the original). 
- The paper doesn't connect (nor do I think it is possible to connect) the metric used here, Hausdorff distance, to any metric between distributions. Therefore it is not clear what value this results have for *generative* models instead of general neural networks.
- The question "In particular, what does it even mean for a GAN to model a distribution?" is trivial. Any mapping on a distribution induces a distribution on its image. While this distribution might be hard/impossible to compute and evaluate in practice, it is clear what it means for a GAN to model a distribution.
- I think the analysis is interesting and should be published but under some revision. If the focus is generative models or GANs, then some thought should be made to the distribution, connecting to metrics between distributions and/or saying something even on a uniform distribution over the manifold embedded in R^n. Otherwise, these results might be worth considering in the more general framework of DNN and maybe see GANs as a single instance. 


Minor details:
- You assume oriantability, but unless I missed something you do not use this assumption anywhere
- While the claim that a compact and connected manifold is geodesically complete is a well known, a reference might be nice as this is a different community. 
- Typo in sec. 7 " is two train two neural networks" -> "is to train two neural networks".

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary: The paper provides certain basic guarantees on when manifolds can be written (exactly or approximately) as the image of a map approximated by a neural net. This is couched as answering the question of when GANs can approximate certain distributions, though in fairness, distributions aren't really ever considered -- only the images of the maps approximated by the neural net of the GAN.  

Technical contributions: The paper mostly stitches together known theorems from (differential) geometry of manifolds, as well as standard universal approximation results. For instance, the result about differentiable connected manifolds proceeds by essentially using known results about the exponential map of such manifolds (Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2), and subsequently approximating this map in a black box way via known universal approximation results. 

Verdict: The paper unfortunately doesn't pass my ICLR bar -- the techniques are essentially known, so there is very little new mathematically; additionally, the question is in some sense the "wrong" one: one needs to approximate *distributions* with support over a low-dimensional manifold, rather than only worry about the range of the map from the latent space to the domain of the GAN. Additionally, much in the way Neural Net approximator has been studied, and one tries to determine which factors require larger nets (e.g. Fourier domain sparsity in Barron's theorem, etc.) the interesting thing here would be to determine what geometric properties of the manifold determine the size of the GAN needed  (e.g. curvature, complexity of the exponential map) and potentially how these properties interact with the distribution over the manifold considered.

content.title: An important research direction
content.comment:
The work discusses the question of universal approximation in the context of generative models.  The results primarily build off of classic universal approximation results.  The novel results in the paper show that there exists a function mapping a simple latent space to any compact connected manifold (the assumed structure of a data manifold).  Then, using the observation that neural networks are capable of universal approximation under some weak assumptions, one may conclude that there exists a network which can approximate this mapping arbitrarily well.  Only the existence of such generative mappings is shown, with no explicit results covering the network architecture, size, or complexity needed to do such an approximation.  Overall, the results confirm the intuitive understanding that by using a sufficiently large network, one has the ability to map a connected compact set (the d-cube) arbitrarily close to the desired compact connected manifold.

The focus and question being addressed in the paper is overall clear.  The question being addressed here is novel in the sense that universal approximation for GANs has not been address previously, while the mathematical techniques are mostly applications of previously developed, somewhat classical results.  

The overall accessibility of the paper for the average reader is good.  From a technical point of view, the clarity of the mathematics is okay.  In particular, several notations, definitions, and proof details have been abbreviated or omitted seemingly due to space constraints. 

The overall impact of the paper is average.  On one hand, it provides a solid first step toward a more refined analysis of universal approximation for GANs - an important research direction.  On the other hand, the results only provide the existence of a certain type of mapping.  These results would be significantly strengthened by providing some guidance on the overall network shape, size, and complexity required to approximate data manifolds belonging to a certain class.

In summary, I think that this work is an important step in the direction of analyzing the approximation properties of GANs and opens the door for further investigation. 

_____
Last, I have listed several presentation/writing suggestions to consider:
1) The overall system for numbering results is difficult to manage as a reader.  Theorem 4.3 comes before corollary 4.1 but both come after theorem 4.1.  This system is used throughout and makes finding results difficult.

2) The notion/notation for the tangent space of a manifold, although clear to more mathematically oriented people, may not be obvious to all.

3) Phi is used both to denote network parameters in the introduction, and later as an activation function.

4) The sentence "For conciseness, we will call nonlinearities satisfying... ...simply universal nonlinearities.", could be clarified.  It took several more pages of reading its meaning became clear to me. 

5) Check spelling - "continuos", "withour", "generatlized", etc.

6) The notation in 5.2, it gets used only once and is never defined.  Same as in comment 2, this notation might be familiar to certain mathematicians, but almost certainly won't stand out as clear within the average reader's knowledge base.

7) At its core, the limitations discussed in this section are that if we use smooth, monotonic activation functions, the generated manifold will be diffeomorphic to the latent space I_d.  To me, it is unclear why this would be a significant limitation when its been assumed that the data manifolds have somewhat nice properties.  Furthermore, it isn't clear to me why this would be surprising behavior to begin with. Perhaps more explanation as to why this is a large limitation could be helpful.

8) Calling a "monotone/monotonic function" a "monotonous function" sounds off.  A monotonous function sounds like a very boring function which never changes.  Calling the functions monotone or monotonic would be the correct phrasing. 

9) In one result, "tensor tensor" should be changed to just "tensor".  Or the wording could be changed entirely, since tensors only are mentioned in this one instance.

10) The vectorization operation called "vec" is taken to be assumed knowledge/notation that everyone is familiar with.  It makes it somewhat difficult to understand exactly what is going on without defining these operations.  Perhaps consider clearly defining this operation in the appendix, since it isn't central to the paper but nonetheless is used.

11) For the paragraph called "Arbitrary stride", it is noted that "The same argument as before [for single stride] applies".  Since limited space seems to be a challenge in this paper, why not just have one argument?

12) Although it is implied by the assumptions, I think it's important to state that the results in section 6 do not apply for ReLU CNNs, since the rest of the results seem generally applicable for ReLU units.

content.title: Official Blind Review #5
content.review:
This paper theoretically shows that data manifolds can be approximated by neural-network-based generative models including GANs. In particular, they prove that under mild assumptions neural networks can map a given latent space $M_z$ onto a set $M_theta$ which is close to the given data manifold $M$ within a small Hausdorff distance. There results hold for the case of both single data manifold (i.e. data generated from a single class) and multiple data manifolds (i.e. data generated from multiple classes). In the latter, they need to allow insignificant parts of the latent space to be mapped onto thin “tunnels” connecting the manifolds. The construction of the mapping from the latent space onto the data manifold provided in their proofs is only for shallow networks. Section 6 of the paper - Invariance Property of Deep Expanding Networks - characterizes the property of the manifold $M_theta$ computed by deep neural networks that expanding the dimensionality of the input. In particular, they show that $M_theta$ is a smooth embedded manifold and it is diffeomorphic to the latent manifold $M_z$, which shows that neural networks cannot significantly transform the latent space. The paper also extends the results for the geometric universality of generative models to cycle generative models including the CycleGANs or Pix2Pix architectures. In particular, they show that under mild conditions, there exists a pair of neural networks that can approximately map back and forth between two given data manifolds.

Potentially, this paper could be an interesting contribution. However, some points in the theory need to be verified, and at least toy experiments should be provided to validate their theoretical claims. Furthermore, Section 6 - Invariance Property of Deep Expanding Networks - does not seem related to the main story of the paper and should be a separate paper itself. I weakly reject this paper, but given these clarifications in an author response, I would be willing to increase the score. 

Main arguments and questions:

1. Theorem 5.1 and 5.2 - Geometric Universality of Generative Models for signal class and multiclass case - seem to be straight-forward applications of Lemma 5.1 and Theorem 4.2. Lemma 5.1 is a special case of the Brown’s mapping theorem and Theorem 4.2 is the well-known theorem on the universal approximation power of neural networks. I, therefore, question the significance of  Theorem 5.1 and 5.2.

2. Since this is clearly a theory paper, lack of experiments can be tolerated. However, the paper does not provide even a single toy simulation result to at least shed light on their theoretical claims. For example, the results from Theorem 6.1 which show that neural networks cannot significantly transform the latent space can be empirically justified.

3. Will the results in Section 5 and 7 hold for Convolutional Neural Networks, or only for Fully Connected Networks? 

4. Theorem 6.1 shows that the manifold $M_theta$ computed by a neural network is diffeomorphic to the latent manifold $M_z$. However, the mappings by deep generative models like GANs, in most cases, are not invertible. It would be great if the authors can elaborate this point more. Otherwise, the results in Theorem 6.1 are questionable. 

5. The paper admits that according to theorem 6.1, “it is impossible to approximate an arbitrary data manifold with latent space being R^{d}”, but in practice, deep generative models like GANs can generate good-looking images. As mentioned in the paper, a precise theorem for this case is not provided. The authors, however, say they “hypothesize that it may be possible to approximate an arbitrary compact data manifold using expanding networks up to a subset of arbitrary small measure, and thus limitations imposed by Theorem 6.1 are negligible in practice.”. However, I didn’t see how this hypothesis is related to the results and discussion in Section 7. It would be great if the authors can provide more explanation for this hypothesis and its connection to the results in Section 7.

6. Geometric universality does not guarantee that a good approximation to data manifolds can be found after training the generative model. The optimization, especially the objective losses used to train the model, plays an important role in understanding the manifold $M_theta$ represented by the trained model. As a result, I am not quite sure about the significance of this paper and would appreciate if the authors can discuss the relevance of their results.

Things to improve the paper that did not impact the score:

1. The paper should define what fully connected neural networks are.

2. Some notations in the paper need to be defined such as the ≃ in Theorem 6.1.

3. More discussion on exponential map and the intuitions behind it should be provided.

Minor comments:

There are some typos in the paper such as “continuos” in page 4, “an embedding is the following” in Definition 6.1, “may possible” in page 7, and “is two train two neural networks” in page 7.
